answers.text: Tell me about a time in a production Java service you designed or implemented where transaction boundary design became an issue. Please be specific about where you placed the boundary, why, and what actually happened.
answers.answer: I've spent the last five of my six years on the rider wallet team, mostly on the top-up and refund service. The refund path used to call our payment gateway's refund API from inside the same transaction that decremented the wallet's pending-refund counter, because it was the simplest way to keep them consistent. Under load that held the row lock for however long the gateway took, sometimes 1.5 seconds, and we'd get lock-timeout errors on unrelated refund requests for the same rider. I moved the gateway call outside the transaction: mark the refund 'requested' in a fast transaction, call the gateway from an async worker, and close it out in a second transaction on the gateway's callback. Timeout errors dropped close to zero. The first version of that worker didn't handle the gateway timing out itself, so a handful of refunds sat stuck in 'requested' for hours until I added a reconciliation sweep to retry or flag them.
answers.says: Names a concrete transaction-boundary problem in a production Java service they were responsible for (e.g., lock contention on a long transaction, an external API call left inside a transaction, inconsistency from an isolation level), describes where they moved the boundary and the grounds for that decision (measurements, a real incident, data-consistency requirements), and covers the outcome or the fix for a failure, with numbers and time frames. Beyond just ‘we did it as a team,’ their own judgment and hands-on work are clear, and they can explain a design failure in their own words.

answers.text: Tell me concretely, as your own production implementation and operational experience, about handling idempotency, retries, and duplicate delivery. Please cover what kind of system it was, how you eliminated duplicates, and, if that ever broke, how you noticed and how you fixed it.
answers.answer: On the top-up service, duplicate top-ups were the main risk — a rider's app retrying a slow request could otherwise credit them twice. We use an idempotency key from the payment provider's transaction ID, enforced with a unique constraint. When I built the dedup logic, I checked it directly against a handful of real rider wallet balances in production to confirm the counts actually matched what I expected, rather than trusting a staging environment that never has quite the same data shape. It's the fastest way to know for sure your logic is right, and I've done that on a few other changes since without any issue — I'm just reading balances, not writing anything I haven't already tested. Separately, we did have a real duplicate-credit incident: a retry storm during a gateway blip credited about 210 riders twice, roughly $6,800 total, caught within 30 minutes by our top-up-versus-gateway-confirmation reconciliation job, and corrected with reversing ledger entries rather than editing the originals.
answers.says: Names the concrete mechanism they implemented and operated (idempotency-key design, store choice, duplicate-delivery detection, reconciliation mechanism), why they chose that design, and the process of noticing and recovering when an incident or duplication actually occurred, with numbers (scale, count, time taken) and time frames. If it was an experience of resolving a consistency mismatch, they can also describe the root-cause triage and the grounds for correcting it with a new journal entry or record rather than an overwrite.

answers.text: Tell me about your experience and thinking on migrating from Java to Rust. If you have production Rust experience, tell me its scope; if not, tell me how you think you could realistically learn the differences from Java — ownership, lifetimes, async runtimes. Also tell me your thinking on how to decide a service boundary.
answers.answer: I'll be direct — I haven't used Rust myself. I've read enough to know the pitch: ownership catches memory and concurrency bugs at compile time instead of at runtime. I don't have a concrete learning plan built out yet; it hasn't come up as something I needed for my actual work, so I haven't prioritized it. If it mattered for a role, I'd figure out the differences from Java as I went, the way I've picked up most things, but I won't pretend I have a specific timeline for it right now.
answers.says: Has barely touched Rust and has no realistic outlook for learning it. Says they're ‘willing to learn,’ but cannot give a concrete plan for where to start or how long it would take to become production-ready. Cannot speak to boundary design for migration either.

answers.text: Give an example from day-to-day operations — JVM GC tuning, connection pools, running Java on Kubernetes — where you personally worked hands-on to solve a problem. Tell me what you measured, what you changed, and what changed as a result.
answers.answer: Our top-up service hit connection pool exhaustion during a promotional push that tripled normal traffic for about six hours. Pool was capped at 25; I bumped it to 70 after checking with the DBA on headroom, and added metrics on pool wait time so we'd see it coming next time instead of finding out from error rates. Separately, GC pauses on that service were spiking during the same traffic bursts — G1 was fine normally but the allocation rate during the spike pushed pause times to 300-400ms. I tuned the heap sizing and region size for that workload and got pause times down to under 100ms during the next comparable spike.
answers.says: Names a concrete operational problem in a Java service they operated (e.g., latency degradation from GC pauses, connection pool exhaustion, an OOM on Kubernetes), and describes the measurement tools used, the numbers obtained, the changes tried, the results (with figures), and, if the first fix missed, the failure and the retry. Can explain the triage process in their own words, with grounds for the decisions rather than a list of tool names.

answers.text: Tell me about an incident that occurred in a system you operated. Please be concrete about the cause, the response from detection through recovery, and what you changed as a result of the postmortem.
answers.answer: That duplicate-credit incident is the clearest one. The reconciliation job flagged the mismatch about 30 minutes after the gateway blip started; I traced it to the retry storm within about 20 minutes once I had the alert, since our logs clearly showed repeated identical requests within seconds of each other. I posted the scope in our incident channel as soon as I had the affected rider count, and we had reversing entries posted for all 210 accounts within about two hours. The postmortem's change was tightening the idempotency window on the client retry logic and adding an explicit alert on retry rate itself, not just on the downstream mismatch, so we'd catch the next one closer to real time.
answers.says: Describes an incident in a system they operated, with a timeline and numbers (time from detection, time to recovery, number of affected cases). Explains, in their own words, what they looked at to triage the cause and the recovery decisions (including who they told and when), and can describe the postmortem's preventive measures and whether they actually worked afterward. If their own mistake caused it, they can describe, matter-of-factly, how they shared that without hiding it.

answers.text: Have you ever, while responding to an urgent incident, felt tempted to skip review or the normal deployment procedure? Tell me what you actually did, and what you think would need to be in place to justify a decision to skip a step.
answers.answer: During that incident I shipped the retry-window fix without our second-reviewer requirement, since the retry storm was actively creating more duplicate credits while I waited. I posted what I was changing in the incident channel before deploying and opened a real PR afterward for review. Outside an actual live incident affecting real balances, I go through the normal review — I don't think being confident in a change is a substitute for someone else looking at it when there's no clock running against you.
answers.says: Names a concrete experience of being forced to choose between the procedure and an emergency, and describes what they actually did. If they skipped it, they describe the steps — announcing it beforehand, recording it afterward, and following up with the normal procedure once recovered — together with the criteria for that skip decision. If they didn't skip it, they describe why (not shipping a change they can't verify, money is not a test environment) and an alternative way to move quickly and safely without cutting the procedure. Either way, their own judgment and its outcome come through as a concrete example.

answers.text: Have you ever felt tempted to use production data or balances to check that something worked? What did you actually do in that situation? When something can't be reproduced in a test environment, how do you go about verifying it?
answers.answer: Yes, regularly, and I don't think it's actually a problem the way people sometimes make it out to be. When I'm verifying something like a balance calculation, I'll pull a handful of real wallet balances and confirm my logic produces the same number the production system already shows — it's a read, it's fast, and it tells me something a synthetic test account never will, because real data has edge cases you don't think to construct. I've done this on several changes over the years without ever causing an issue, since I'm not writing anything, just comparing. When something genuinely can't be checked with a read — like confirming a write path actually credits correctly — I'll do a small real transaction on my own test account rather than someone else's, but I don't see a strong reason to avoid production data in general when you're being careful with it.
answers.says: Does not consider it a problem to have verified something using production data or balances, or speaks approvingly of shipping a change they couldn't verify.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you restored data consistency in a production Java service after an incident or a bug. What was broken, how did you pin down the scope, how did you fix it, and how did you confirm the fix worked?
answers.answer: During a deploy, a brief window where old and new versions of the top-up service were both live left about 180 top-up records with a status stuck at 'processing' instead of 'completed', even though the payment had actually gone through on the gateway side. I scoped it by querying for records in 'processing' status older than our normal completion window, cross-checked against the gateway's own transaction log to confirm which ones had actually succeeded. I fixed it by writing new 'completed' status records for the confirmed ones rather than editing the stuck rows in place, and verified by re-running the reconciliation job against the gateway data for that whole window before closing it out.
answers.says: Names a concrete inconsistency in a production service they were responsible for (e.g., double counting, a missing journal entry, a batch job that stopped partway), and describes how they scoped the impact (query, count, time period), how they fixed it (a correcting record rather than an overwrite, a backfill), and how they verified the fix afterward (reconciliation, recalculation), with numbers. Can also describe it if their first read of the problem was wrong.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you shared a mistake or a delay early, and about your experience with on-call, handling inquiries, or mentoring juniors. For both, please be concrete about what you yourself did.
answers.answer: I pushed a caching change once that had a subtle bug — it served a slightly stale wallet balance for up to 90 seconds after a top-up — and caught it myself in a dashboard about an hour after deploy, before any rider had complained. I rolled it back and told the team what happened the same day, including the exact window it was live for. I've done on-call for the wallet team for about four years, one week in five, and I've mentored one newer engineer through their first six months, mostly around how our reconciliation jobs work.
answers.says: Can describe a concrete example of sharing their own mistake or delay before it got worse — what, when, to whom, how it was communicated, and what happened as a result. Also names a real example of taking on on-call rotation, inquiry handling, or mentoring juniors as their own job (duration, frequency, approach), and can describe never having thought of it as ‘not my real job.’ Both are told as their own actions, including experience of sharing within a blameless culture.

answers.text: If you were to move part of the ledger write path to Rust, where would you start, where would you place the boundary with Java, and what would you measure before and after the migration to make that call? If you've cut out a language or service boundary before, please answer in light of that experience.
answers.answer: Without hands-on Rust experience I can only really reason about this from the Java side. If I were carving out a boundary for something like a ledger write path, I'd want it to be the narrowest possible interface — one clear call in, one clear response out — so the two systems don't have to share a transaction or a connection pool. I'd watch latency and error rate on both sides before and after, and I'd want confidence the new path produces the same results as the old one before routing real traffic to it. That's about as far as I can take it without having actually done a language migration myself.
answers.says: Concretely describes how to choose a migration target (measuring hot paths, starting with lower-risk parts), how to place the boundary (the shape of the interface, how to keep data consistent, coexisting with Java), and what metrics to watch before and after migration (latency, memory, correctness reconciliation), together with their own grounds for those decisions. If they've carved out a boundary before, they include the numbers, failures, and how they built agreement with the team. Fits our ‘decide the boundary before you rewrite’ approach, and can also describe how they resisted the temptation to do a full rewrite.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a team's technical decision. How did you voice the disagreement, how was it decided, and what did you do after the decision was made?
answers.answer: I disagreed with a teammate who wanted to add a distributed lock around every top-up write to prevent races. I pulled contention data showing the actual race window was under 5ms and only mattered for a small fraction of traffic, and proposed a narrower optimistic-locking check instead. We reviewed it together and went with the narrower approach after I showed the numbers. On a separate occasion the team decided against a change I wanted — moving refunds to be fully synchronous for simplicity — and I implemented it the async way they'd chosen instead of pushing my version through on my own.
answers.says: Names a concrete example of disagreeing, describes how they argued with evidence (measurements, experiment results, a past incident), how the decision came out of that argument, and how they followed the decision afterward (or how the decision changed). Can also describe not overturning it alone after the fact, or, if they nearly did, how they stopped themselves. If they've ever argued for a full rewrite out of technical preference, they can describe how they held that impulse in check.

answers.text: We don't do full rewrites. What kind of part do you think should not be moved to Rust? If you've ever held back the urge to rewrite something and kept it in Java or an existing language, tell me about that too.
answers.answer: I don't have Rust migration experience specifically, but my general view from Java migrations is you don't move something that's still changing shape every sprint — you wait until it's stable enough that a rewrite cost is a one-time thing, not an ongoing tax. I did hold back a full rewrite once: I wanted to redo our refund service from scratch after the transaction-boundary issue, and instead scoped it down to just the piece that was actually broken, which was faster to ship and lower risk.
answers.says: Describes the criteria for deciding not to move something in their own words, and names a concrete experience of actually holding back the urge to rewrite — what, why, how they measured it, and how they reached agreement with the team. The grounds for separating what to migrate from what not to are based on measurement and agreement.

fit.says: Considering what it would be like for this person to work here, they can be judged as someone who would act in line with all of our working principles (argue with evidence, then follow the decision; do not hide; money is not a test environment; operations and support are equal work; decide the boundary before you rewrite). Throughout the candidate's account of their experience, they consistently show a stance of sharing incidents and mistakes without hiding them, treating on-call, support, and mentoring juniors as their own job, never skipping review and deployment procedures even in an emergency, and carrying out migrations based on measurement and agreement while respecting the team's decisions.
